title: Scientific notation to an ordinary number

primary_objective.statement: Turn a number such as 3.2 × 10⁴ or 4.5 × 10⁻³ into an ordinary number by moving the decimal point.

teach.text: Scientific notation writes a number as a number from 1 up to (but not including) 10, times a power of 10. It keeps very large and very small numbers short: 32,000 is 3.2 × 10⁴.

To turn it back into an ordinary number, move the decimal point. A positive exponent moves it to the right that many places, making the number bigger. A negative exponent moves it to the left, making the number smaller.
A size check helps: 10³ is a thousand and 10⁻³ is a thousandth. If the exponent is negative, your answer must be less than 1 (for a coefficient below 10).

alternate_explanations.text: Think of the exponent as a count of multiplications by 10 (positive) or divisions by 10 (negative). 4.5 divided by 10 three times is 0.45, then 0.045, then 0.0045.

checks.feedback: A negative exponent moves the point left: 7.1 → 0.71 → 0.071. Moving it right instead gives 710, which is far too big.
A positive exponent moves the point right 5 places: 9 becomes 900,000. Moving left would give a tiny number instead.
Move the point 1 place left: 1.5 becomes 0.15.

misconceptions.label: moving the decimal point the wrong way
misconceptions.contrast: A positive power of ten makes a number bigger, so the point moves right; a negative power makes it smaller, so the point moves left. Check the size: 7.1 × 10⁻² must be less than 1, so 710 cannot be right.

return_cue: Back to your lesson: positive exponent, move the point right; negative exponent, move it left.
